metadata.description: CI workflow abuse (pull_request_target) exposing npm publish token, leading to trojanized Nx packages with QUIETVAULT credential-stealing payload. Development vector (#10.2): consumers pulled trojanized versions during dependency installation.

path.description: Attacker submits a pull request to the Nx monorepo — a legitimate GitHub function. The pull_request_target workflow runs with base-repo privileges and permits untrusted PR code to execute with access to secrets. No bug, no exploit — the CI system does what it was configured to do. Excessive scope of a legitimate function.
path.evidence: Nx post-mortem disclosure; Sysdig TRT analysis.

path.description: CI pipeline executes attacker's code via GitHub Actions' intended execution capability. R-EXEC: foreign code, designed mechanism. Payload extracts the npm publishing token from CI secrets.

dre.title: npm Publish Token Stolen
dre.desc: npm publishing token extracted from CI environment secrets. Enabling cluster: #7.

path.evidence: Palo Alto Unit 42 analysis; ReversingLabs report.

path.description: Attacker uses the stolen npm token to authenticate as the Nx maintainer. R-CRED: credential use is always #4 regardless of acquisition method.
Trojanized versions of nx and related packages published via legitimate npm publish command. The publish API works as designed. Package integrity compromised.

dre.title: Nx Package Integrity Compromised
dre.desc: Trojanized versions of nx and related packages published to npm registry.

path.evidence: npm security advisory; ReversingLabs package analysis.

path.description: Trust Acceptance Event (Development Vector / #10.2). Consumers pull the trojanized Nx version during dependency installation. npm serves as transit infrastructure with its own control surface.

Consumer's package manager resolves, downloads, unpacks, and processes the package — preparing the lifecycle hook environment. Controls: namespace restrictions, registry allowlists, install sandboxing, --ignore-scripts.
QUIETVAULT payload executes via postinstall lifecycle hook on the consumer's machine. R-EXEC: FEC execution via designed lifecycle hook mechanism.

Payload uses standard filesystem APIs and environment variable access to harvest credentials: .npmrc, .gitconfig, AWS credential files, GCP JSON keys. Data stays data — no foreign code introduced. Legitimate functions, abused scope.

dre.title: Credential Filesystem Sweep
dre.desc: npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS credentials, and GCP service account keys harvested from consumer's filesystem.

path.evidence: Sysdig TRT; credential file paths enumerated in QUIETVAULT payload.

path.description: QUIETVAULT downloads and executes TruffleHog for deeper credential scanning. In some instances, weaponizes an LLM coding assistant already present on the victim's machine. R-EXEC: separate #7 step — downloading/invoking secondary tools is a foreign-code event.
path.evidence: TruffleHog binary download observed; LLM weaponization variant documented by Palo Alto Unit 42.

path.description: Exfiltration via legitimate GitHub APIs: malware creates a public repository and commits stolen credential data. The APIs function as designed; their scope is abused.

dre.title: Credential Exfiltration via GitHub
dre.desc: Stolen credentials committed to attacker-controlled public GitHub repository.

bizRisk.title: Cascading Credential Exposure
bizRisk.desc: Exfiltrated credentials (npm, GitHub, AWS, GCP) enable lateral attacks across multiple services and organizations.

path.evidence: Public GitHub repos created by QUIETVAULT observed and reported.
